# WHY OUR TEAM SWITCHED TO WEEKLY PLANNING

For years we planned in monthly cycles. It felt efficient: one big meeting, one big document, and then everyone went off to execute. In practice, by week two the plan was already out of date.

## THE PROBLEM

Monthly plans assumed we knew what the month would bring. We never did. Client requests, bugs, and hiring all arrived on their own schedule.

## WHAT WE CHANGED

1. Every Monday, a 30-minute planning call.
2. Each person commits to three outcomes, not tasks.
3. Friday, a short written recap of what shipped and what slipped, and why.

The results after one quarter: fewer missed deadlines, and far less time spent re-planning in the middle of the month. See the template we use at www.example.com/weekly-template.

# How We Cut Our Office Electricity Bill by 30% This Summer

Every June our electricity bill jumps, and every June we tell ourselves we'll "look into it." This year we actually did — and the results surprised us.

Here's the short version:

- Cooling was 70% of the bill
- Most of it ran when nobody was in the office
- Three cheap changes fixed most of it

It worked.

## WHERE THE ENERGY WAS GOING

We borrowed a plug-in energy meter and logged usage for two weeks. The pattern was obvious once we saw it: the AC units ran at full power from 6am to 11pm, even though the office is empty after 6pm.

Other culprits we found:

- Two old fridges in the pantry (one was completely empty)
- Monitors left on standby over the weekend
- The server-room AC, set to 18°C "just to be safe"
- Printers that never go to sleep

What we changed:

1. Put every AC unit on a timer: on at 7:30am, off at 6pm, and off entirely on Fridays and Saturdays.
2. Raised the thermostat from 21°C to 24°C. After the first week, nobody noticed.
3. Unplugged the spare fridge & replaced the other with an efficient model.
4. Set monitors and printers to sleep after 15 minutes.

Note: we checked the server room with our IT provider before touching it. Don't skip that step — some equipment really does need cooler air.

## The Results

July's bill was 31% lower than last July's, even though it was a hotter month. The timers cost less than 60 rials in total and paid for themselves in under three weeks.

Want to try this yourself?  The meter we used is listed at https://www.example.com/energy-meter, and the government's efficiency guide is at www.example.org/save-energy.

# How to Choose a Home Coffee Grinder in 2026

If you've ever wondered why the coffee at your favourite café tastes better than what you make at home, the answer is usually not the beans or the machine. It's the grinder. A consistent grind is the single biggest upgrade most home brewers can make, and it doesn't have to cost a fortune.

In this guide we'll walk through the two main grinder types, what grind size you need for each brewing method, and a few models worth considering at different budgets.

![A burr coffee grinder on a kitchen counter next to a bag of whole beans](https://picsum.photos/seed/grinder-hero/1200/700 "A good burr grinder is the foundation of better coffee at home.")

## Blade vs Burr Grinders

Blade grinders work like a small blender. A spinning blade chops the beans into pieces of wildly different sizes, some almost powder and some still chunky. That mix extracts unevenly, which is why blade-ground coffee often tastes bitter and sour at the same time.

Burr grinders crush beans between two abrasive surfaces set a fixed distance apart. Every particle comes out close to the same size, so extraction is even and the flavour is cleaner. There are two kinds of burrs:

- Conical burrs: quieter, slower, retain less heat, usually cheaper
- Flat burrs: more uniform grind, favoured for espresso, usually pricier and louder

## Grind Size by Brewing Method

The right grind depends entirely on how you brew. Use this table as a starting point and adjust by taste.

| Brewing Method | Grind Size | Texture Comparison | Brew Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Turkish | Extra fine | Flour | 3-4 min |
| Espresso | Fine | Table salt | 25-30 sec |
| AeroPress | Fine-medium | Fine sand | 1-2 min |
| Pour over (V60) | Medium-fine | Coarse sand | 2.5-3.5 min |
| Drip machine | Medium | Regular sand | 4-6 min |
| French press | Coarse | Sea salt | 4 min |
| Cold brew | Extra coarse | Peppercorns | 12-24 hours |

![Five small piles of ground coffee arranged from extra fine to extra coarse](https://picsum.photos/seed/grind-sizes/1000/600 "From left to right: extra fine, fine, medium, coarse, extra coarse.")

## Grinders Worth Considering

Below are four grinders across different price points. Prices are approximate retail in OMR and will vary by store.

| Model | Type | Burr | Price (OMR) | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hario Skerton Pro | Manual | Conical ceramic | 22 | Travel and French press |
| Baratza Encore ESP | Electric | Conical steel | 78 | Pour over and beginner espresso |
| Fellow Opus | Electric | Conical steel | 75 | All-rounder, drip to espresso |
| Niche Zero | Electric | Conical steel | 260 | Serious espresso at home |

## How to Get the Most From Your Grinder

1. Grind right before brewing. Ground coffee loses aroma within minutes.
2. Start at the manufacturer's recommended setting, then adjust one step at a time.
3. Clean the burrs every few weeks with a brush or grinder cleaning tablets.
4. Weigh your beans instead of using scoops for repeatable results.

![Hot water being poured over fresh coffee grounds in a pour-over dripper](https://picsum.photos/seed/pour-over/1200/800 "Freshly ground coffee blooming in a pour-over dripper.")

## Final Thoughts

You don't need the most expensive grinder to taste a difference. Moving from a blade grinder to even an entry-level burr grinder will change your morning cup more than any new machine or fancy bean. Pick one that matches how you brew, keep it clean, and grind fresh every time.

# Why AI Is Good for Us: The Case for Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence gets a lot of headlines, and not all of them are kind. But behind the noise, AI is quietly doing useful work in hospitals, laboratories, classrooms and offices. It speeds up tasks that used to take days, catches things people miss, and opens up tools that were once only available to large organisations.

This post looks at what AI actually is, where it is already helping, and why, used well, it is a net positive.

![Diagram of an artificial neural network with an input layer, a hidden layer and an output layer, connected by arrows](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Colored_neural_network.svg/1280px-Colored_neural_network.svg.png "Most modern AI is built on neural networks: layers of simple units that learn patterns from examples. Credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0")

## What We Mean by AI

At its core, modern AI is software that learns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Show a system enough labelled X-rays, sentences or photos, and it learns to recognise the patterns in them. That one idea powers everything from spam filters to translation apps to tools that help scientists design new medicines.

## AI Has Improved Remarkably Fast

A good illustration is the ImageNet challenge, a yearly competition where systems had to identify objects in over a million photos. In 2010 the best system got the answer wrong more than a quarter of the time. By 2015 the winning system was making fewer mistakes than the commonly cited human estimate on the same test.

The same pattern of rapid improvement has since repeated in speech recognition, translation, writing and scientific modelling.

## Where AI Is Already Helping

AI is most valuable when it takes on work that is repetitive, slow or too large for people to do by hand, and frees people up for the parts that need judgement.

| Field | What AI Does | Why It Matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Healthcare | Flags possible problems in scans and X-rays | Helps doctors prioritise urgent cases |
| Science | Predicts the 3D shape of proteins | Speeds up drug and disease research |
| Accessibility | Live captions, image descriptions, text-to-speech | Opens content to people with disabilities |
| Education | Explains topics at each student's own pace | Personal tutoring for more learners |
| Agriculture | Spots crop disease from photos | Earlier treatment, less crop loss |
| Business | Summarises documents and drafts routine replies | Hours saved on repetitive work |
| Language | Translates text and speech instantly | Makes it easier to talk across languages |

![3D ribbon model of a protein structure predicted by AlphaFold](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a4/C12orf29_AlphaFold.png "A protein structure predicted by AlphaFold. Working out shapes like this used to take researchers months or years. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## Key Milestones

| Year | Milestone | Why It Mattered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1997 | IBM Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov | First time a computer beat a reigning world champion in a match |
| 2012 | AlexNet wins the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin | Kicked off the deep learning era |
| 2016 | DeepMind's AlphaGo beats Go champion Lee Sedol | Mastered a game long thought too complex for computers |
| 2020 | AlphaFold 2 tops the CASP14 protein structure assessment | Largely solved a 50-year-old problem in biology |
| 2022 | OpenAI releases ChatGPT | Brought conversational AI to the general public |
| 2024 | Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded partly for AlphaFold | Formal recognition of AI's scientific contribution |

![IBM Deep Blue computer on display at the Computer History Museum](<https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/IBM_Deep_Blue_at_Computer_History_Museum_(9361685537).jpg> "IBM's Deep Blue, which beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, now on display at the Computer History Museum. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## Why It's a Net Positive

1. It saves time. Tasks like summarising a long report or sorting thousands of records take minutes instead of days.
2. It improves consistency. An AI system doesn't get tired at the end of a shift, which makes it a strong second pair of eyes.
3. It widens access. Tutoring, translation and expert-level explanations are no longer limited to people who can pay for them.
4. It speeds up discovery. Scientists can test ideas in software before spending months in the lab.
5. It lets people focus on judgement. When AI handles the routine parts, humans can spend their time on decisions, creativity and care.

## The Best Results Come From AI and People Working Together

The strongest use of AI is not replacing people but working alongside them. The AI produces a first draft, a flag or a prediction; a person reviews it, corrects it and makes the final call. Those corrections then help the system get better over time.

![A radiologist reviewing medical scans on computer monitors](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Radiologist_in_San_Diego_CA_2010.jpg "AI tools can flag scans that need a closer look, but the diagnosis stays with the doctor. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## A Fair Word on the Limits

AI is not perfect. It can be confidently wrong, it can reflect biases in the data it learned from, and it raises real questions about privacy, jobs and who is accountable when things go wrong. These are serious issues, and they are the reason human oversight matters. Being optimistic about AI doesn't mean ignoring these problems; it means building and using it carefully.

## Final Thoughts

AI is a tool, and like any powerful tool its value depends on how it is used. Used thoughtfully, with people staying in charge of the decisions that matter, it can make work faster, knowledge more accessible and science more ambitious. That is a future worth building.

For years we planned in monthly cycles. It felt efficient: one big meeting, one big document, and then everyone went off to execute. In practice, by week two the plan was already out of date.

## THE PROBLEM

Monthly plans assumed we knew what the month would bring. We never did. Client requests, bugs, and hiring all arrived on their own schedule.

## WHAT WE CHANGED

1. Every Monday, a 30-minute planning call.
2. Each person commits to three outcomes, not tasks.
3. Friday, a short written recap of what shipped and what slipped, and why.

The results after one quarter: fewer missed deadlines, and far less time spent re-planning in the middle of the month. See the template we use at www.example.com/weekly-template.

If you try it, tell us how it goes.

# How We Cut Our Office Electricity Bill by 30% This Summer

Every June our electricity bill jumps, and every June we tell ourselves we'll "look into it." This year we actually did — and the results surprised us.

Here's the short version:

- Cooling was 70% of the bill
- Most of it ran when nobody was in the office
- Three cheap changes fixed most of it

It worked.

## WHERE THE ENERGY WAS GOING

We borrowed a plug-in energy meter and logged usage for two weeks. The pattern was obvious once we saw it: the AC units ran at full power from 6am to 11pm, even though the office is empty after 6pm.

Other culprits we found:

- Two old fridges in the pantry (one was completely empty)
- Monitors left on standby over the weekend
- The server-room AC, set to 18°C "just to be safe"
- Printers that never go to sleep

What we changed:

1. Put every AC unit on a timer: on at 7:30am, off at 6pm, and off entirely on Fridays and Saturdays.
2. Raised the thermostat from 21°C to 24°C. After the first week, nobody noticed.
3. Unplugged the spare fridge & replaced the other with an efficient model.
4. Set monitors and printers to sleep after 15 minutes.

Note: we checked the server room with our IT provider before touching it. Don't skip that step — some equipment really does need cooler air.

## The Results

July's bill was 31% lower than last July's, even though it was a hotter month. The timers cost less than 60 rials in total and paid for themselves in under three weeks.

Want to try this yourself?  The meter we used is listed at https://www.example.com/energy-meter, and the government's efficiency guide is at www.example.org/save-energy.

If you have questions, visit us or write to us:

Office 204, Al Khuwair Business Tower\

Muscat, Sultanate of Oman

Thanks for reading!

— The Operations Team

# How to Choose a Home Coffee Grinder in 2026

If you've ever wondered why the coffee at your favourite café tastes better than what you make at home, the answer is usually not the beans or the machine. It's the grinder. A consistent grind is the single biggest upgrade most home brewers can make, and it doesn't have to cost a fortune.

In this guide we'll walk through the two main grinder types, what grind size you need for each brewing method, and a few models worth considering at different budgets.

![A burr coffee grinder on a kitchen counter next to a bag of whole beans](https://picsum.photos/seed/grinder-hero/1200/700 "A good burr grinder is the foundation of better coffee at home.")

## Blade vs Burr Grinders

Blade grinders work like a small blender. A spinning blade chops the beans into pieces of wildly different sizes, some almost powder and some still chunky. That mix extracts unevenly, which is why blade-ground coffee often tastes bitter and sour at the same time.

Burr grinders crush beans between two abrasive surfaces set a fixed distance apart. Every particle comes out close to the same size, so extraction is even and the flavour is cleaner. There are two kinds of burrs:

- Conical burrs: quieter, slower, retain less heat, usually cheaper
- Flat burrs: more uniform grind, favoured for espresso, usually pricier and louder

## Grind Size by Brewing Method

The right grind depends entirely on how you brew. Use this table as a starting point and adjust by taste.

| Brewing Method | Grind Size | Texture Comparison | Brew Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Turkish | Extra fine | Flour | 3-4 min |
| Espresso | Fine | Table salt | 25-30 sec |
| AeroPress | Fine-medium | Fine sand | 1-2 min |
| Pour over (V60) | Medium-fine | Coarse sand | 2.5-3.5 min |
| Drip machine | Medium | Regular sand | 4-6 min |
| French press | Coarse | Sea salt | 4 min |
| Cold brew | Extra coarse | Peppercorns | 12-24 hours |

![Five small piles of ground coffee arranged from extra fine to extra coarse](https://picsum.photos/seed/grind-sizes/1000/600 "From left to right: extra fine, fine, medium, coarse, extra coarse.")

## Grinders Worth Considering

Below are four grinders across different price points. Prices are approximate retail in OMR and will vary by store.

| Model | Type | Burr | Price (OMR) | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hario Skerton Pro | Manual | Conical ceramic | 22 | Travel and French press |
| Baratza Encore ESP | Electric | Conical steel | 78 | Pour over and beginner espresso |
| Fellow Opus | Electric | Conical steel | 75 | All-rounder, drip to espresso |
| Niche Zero | Electric | Conical steel | 260 | Serious espresso at home |

## How to Get the Most From Your Grinder

1. Grind right before brewing. Ground coffee loses aroma within minutes.
2. Start at the manufacturer's recommended setting, then adjust one step at a time.
3. Clean the burrs every few weeks with a brush or grinder cleaning tablets.
4. Weigh your beans instead of using scoops for repeatable results.

![Hot water being poured over fresh coffee grounds in a pour-over dripper](https://picsum.photos/seed/pour-over/1200/800 "Freshly ground coffee blooming in a pour-over dripper.")

## Final Thoughts

You don't need the most expensive grinder to taste a difference. Moving from a blade grinder to even an entry-level burr grinder will change your morning cup more than any new machine or fancy bean. Pick one that matches how you brew, keep it clean, and grind fresh every time.

# Why AI Is Good for Us: The Case for Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence gets a lot of headlines, and not all of them are kind. But behind the noise, AI is quietly doing useful work in hospitals, laboratories, classrooms and offices. It speeds up tasks that used to take days, catches things people miss, and opens up tools that were once only available to large organisations.

This post looks at what AI actually is, where it is already helping, and why, used well, it is a net positive.

![Diagram of an artificial neural network with an input layer, a hidden layer and an output layer, connected by arrows](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Colored_neural_network.svg/1280px-Colored_neural_network.svg.png "Most modern AI is built on neural networks: layers of simple units that learn patterns from examples. Credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0")

## What We Mean by AI

At its core, modern AI is software that learns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Show a system enough labelled X-rays, sentences or photos, and it learns to recognise the patterns in them. That one idea powers everything from spam filters to translation apps to tools that help scientists design new medicines.

## AI Has Improved Remarkably Fast

A good illustration is the ImageNet challenge, a yearly competition where systems had to identify objects in over a million photos. In 2010 the best system got the answer wrong more than a quarter of the time. By 2015 the winning system was making fewer mistakes than the commonly cited human estimate on the same test.

The same pattern of rapid improvement has since repeated in speech recognition, translation, writing and scientific modelling.

## Where AI Is Already Helping

AI is most valuable when it takes on work that is repetitive, slow or too large for people to do by hand, and frees people up for the parts that need judgement.

| Field | What AI Does | Why It Matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Healthcare | Flags possible problems in scans and X-rays | Helps doctors prioritise urgent cases |
| Science | Predicts the 3D shape of proteins | Speeds up drug and disease research |
| Accessibility | Live captions, image descriptions, text-to-speech | Opens content to people with disabilities |
| Education | Explains topics at each student's own pace | Personal tutoring for more learners |
| Agriculture | Spots crop disease from photos | Earlier treatment, less crop loss |
| Business | Summarises documents and drafts routine replies | Hours saved on repetitive work |
| Language | Translates text and speech instantly | Makes it easier to talk across languages |

![3D ribbon model of a protein structure predicted by AlphaFold](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a4/C12orf29_AlphaFold.png "A protein structure predicted by AlphaFold. Working out shapes like this used to take researchers months or years. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## Key Milestones

| Year | Milestone | Why It Mattered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1997 | IBM Deep Blue beats world chess champion Garry Kasparov | First time a computer beat a reigning world champion in a match |
| 2012 | AlexNet wins the ImageNet challenge by a wide margin | Kicked off the deep learning era |
| 2016 | DeepMind's AlphaGo beats Go champion Lee Sedol | Mastered a game long thought too complex for computers |
| 2020 | AlphaFold 2 tops the CASP14 protein structure assessment | Largely solved a 50-year-old problem in biology |
| 2022 | OpenAI releases ChatGPT | Brought conversational AI to the general public |
| 2024 | Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded partly for AlphaFold | Formal recognition of AI's scientific contribution |

![IBM Deep Blue computer on display at the Computer History Museum](<https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/IBM_Deep_Blue_at_Computer_History_Museum_(9361685537).jpg> "IBM's Deep Blue, which beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, now on display at the Computer History Museum. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## Why It's a Net Positive

1. It saves time. Tasks like summarising a long report or sorting thousands of records take minutes instead of days.
2. It improves consistency. An AI system doesn't get tired at the end of a shift, which makes it a strong second pair of eyes.
3. It widens access. Tutoring, translation and expert-level explanations are no longer limited to people who can pay for them.
4. It speeds up discovery. Scientists can test ideas in software before spending months in the lab.
5. It lets people focus on judgement. When AI handles the routine parts, humans can spend their time on decisions, creativity and care.

## The Best Results Come From AI and People Working Together

The strongest use of AI is not replacing people but working alongside them. The AI produces a first draft, a flag or a prediction; a person reviews it, corrects it and makes the final call. Those corrections then help the system get better over time.

![A radiologist reviewing medical scans on computer monitors](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Radiologist_in_San_Diego_CA_2010.jpg "AI tools can flag scans that need a closer look, but the diagnosis stays with the doctor. Credit: Wikimedia Commons")

## A Fair Word on the Limits

AI is not perfect. It can be confidently wrong, it can reflect biases in the data it learned from, and it raises real questions about privacy, jobs and who is accountable when things go wrong. These are serious issues, and they are the reason human oversight matters. Being optimistic about AI doesn't mean ignoring these problems; it means building and using it carefully.

## Final Thoughts

AI is a tool, and like any powerful tool its value depends on how it is used. Used thoughtfully, with people staying in charge of the decisions that matter, it can make work faster, knowledge more accessible and science more ambitious. That is a future worth building.

Those corrections then help the system get better over time. https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Radiologist_in_San_Diego_CA_2010.jpg A radiologist reviewing medical scans on computer monitors AI tools can flag scans that need a closer look, but the diagnosis stays with the doctor. Credit: Wikimedia Commons A Fair Word on the Limits AI is not perfect. It can be confidently wrong, it can reflect biases in the data it learned from, and it raises real questions about privacy, jobs and who is accountable when things go wrong. These are serious issues, and they are the reason human oversight matters. Being optimistic about AI doesn't mean ignoring these problems; it means building and using it carefully. Final Thoughts AI is a tool, and like any powerful tool its value depends on how it is used. Used thoughtfully, with people staying in charge of the decisions that matter, it can make work faster, knowledge more accessible and science more ambitious. That is a future worth building.
